Preserver
pree-ZUR-vur
n. (one who keeps from harm or destruction; a title of God spoken by Job)
From Latin praeservare, to guard beforehand — prae-, before, and servare, to keep or watch. In Job it renders a participle of Hebrew natsar, to watch, guard, keep.

Biblical Definition

Job says it from the bottom of his affliction, and that is what gives the title its weight: I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men? why hast thou set me as a mark against thee, so that I am a burden to myself? He is not paying a compliment. He is confessing that the God who has made him a target is the same God who keeps men alive, and he cannot get away from either fact. That is the honest position of a sufferer who has not let go of doctrine. Elsewhere the preserving is stated flatly and warmly: The LORD shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul; he preserveth the souls of his saints and delivereth them out of the hand of the wicked. Nehemiah's prayer widens it to everything that exists — thou hast made heaven and earth and the seas and all that is therein, and thou preservest them all. So preservation is a doctrine of two ranges. God upholds all things by the word of his power, so that no creature holds itself in being for a moment; and God keeps his own people, so that none is lost. Job had lost nearly everything and still addressed him by the title. That is the point of the book.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one who preserves; one who saves or defends from destruction or evil; that which preserves.

expand to see more

PRESERVER, n. One who preserves; one who saves or defends from destruction or evil.

PRESERVE, v.t. To keep or save from injury or destruction; to defend from evil.

PRESERVATION, n. The act of preserving or keeping safe; the act of keeping from injury, destruction or decay.

UPHOLD, v.t. To lift on high; to elevate; to support; to sustain; to keep from falling.

MARK, n. A visible line made by drawing one substance on another; a butt; anything to be aimed at.

Key Scripture

Job 7:20 — "I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men? why hast thou set me as a mark against thee, so that I am a burden to myself?"

Psalm 121:7 — "The LORD shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul."

Psalm 97:10 — "Ye that love the LORD, hate evil: he preserveth the souls of his saints; he delivereth them out of the hand of the wicked."

Hebrews 11:6 — "But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him."

Modern Corruption

Preservation is read as a promise of comfortable circumstances; Job speaks the title while covered in boils, and the Psalm that promises it is sung by pilgrims walking exposed roads.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's preserving of his people is not a guarantee of their circumstances. Psalm 121 is a song of degrees, sung by men on the road to Jerusalem where the hills held robbers, and it does not promise an easy journey — it promises a keeper who does not sleep. The same God who preserves the soul let Job lose his children, and let Stephen be stoned, and let the apostles be beaten, and never once broke the promise. What is preserved is the soul, and the preserving is proved not by the absence of the arrow but by the survival of the man.

The doctrine has a second range that steadies the first. Nehemiah's prayer says God made heaven and earth and preservest them all, and Hebrews says the Son upholds all things by the word of his power. Creation is not a machine wound up and left running; it continues because it is continually held. Once that is seen, the personal promise stops sounding sentimental. The arm that keeps the stars in their courses is the arm underneath a believer, and Job, who could not understand what was happening to him, still knew whose arm it was.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew natsar (H5341), to watch, guard, keep; shamar (H8104), to keep or preserve; chayah (H2421), to keep alive; Greek phero (G5342), to bear or uphold.

expand to see more

Hebrew natsar (H5341) — to watch over, to guard; the participle Job addresses as preserver of men.

Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep; the repeated verb of Psalm 121, six times in eight verses.

Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to preserve alive; used of Joseph in Egypt, sent before his brethren to save life.

Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, carry, uphold; the Son upholding all things by the word of his power.

Greek tereo (G5083) — to keep, to guard; Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me.

Usage

"“O thou preserver of men” — spoken by a man on an ash heap."

"“he shall preserve thy soul” — the promise stated without qualification."

"“he preserveth the souls of his saints” — the keeping that outlasts the circumstance."
